title: The Art of Investing | François Rochon | Talks at Google
description:
François Rochon speaks about key lessons from his multiple decades experience in value investing.

About François Rochon: 
Francois Rochon was educated as an engineer at the École Polytechnique of Montreal.  After graduating with his Masters Degree (in Science), he worked as a researcher and network engineer for INRS-Telecom and Teleglobe Canada. Following his lifelong passion for investing, he decided to focus his career on professional money management.  After managing family accounts between 1993 and 1996, he joined Montrusco & Associates as an analyst and was then promoted to Portfolio Manager.  At Montrusco, Francois managed US accounts totaling more than $250 million. In December 1998, Francois founded Giverny Capital in order to offer investment management services to clients based on his investment philosophy of owning outstanding companies for the long term. He also sits on various boards of directors.

Moderated by Saurabh Madaan.
summary: The speaker argues that investors should focus on businesses with wide, recurring moats and protected growth prospects, citing Visa and Google as examples of stable, entrenched companies. Conversely, the speaker highlights risks in businesses reliant on frequent product cycles, such as Apple, and notes that high valuations can be justified only when growth is visible far into the future. While the speaker owns shares in various companies like Berkshire Hathaway and Mastercard, they emphasize that owning a conglomerate is not a substitute for buying a specific good business directly.

claims.quote: And sometimes we think the company has lots of room to grow, and it's just like a Starbucks, where they just have to clone the concept that they have built.
claims.speaker: FRANCOIS ROCHON

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that price to book is a better way to value Berkshire Hathaway due to erratic earnings.
claims.quote: Well, in terms of for Berkshire or Markel, probably a price to book is a better-- it's not perfect, but it's probably a better-- way to value.
claims.speaker: FRANCOIS ROCHON

claims.quote: One of the questions I wanted to ask you was, you were showing us this chart about Walt Disney and buying it at 24 times earnings, right? How do you pay up for good businesses?

claims.claim: The speaker owns a few shares of MasterCard just to follow the company, but prefers Visa.
claims.quote: And MasterCard, we own a few shares just to follow it. But we think both companies are great. These are fantastic businesses. We prefer Visa.
claims.speaker: FRANCOIS ROCHON

claims.claim: The speaker prefers Visa over MasterCard and believes it warrants a high P/E ratio due to its protected growth prospects.
claims.quote: Yeah, well, that's a very easy-- we prefer Visa, obviously. And MasterCard, we own a few shares just to follow it. But we think both companies are great. These are fantastic businesses. We prefer Visa.
claims.speaker: FRANCOIS ROCHON

claims.claim: The speaker believes Visa has the most protected business for many years and warrants a high P/E ratio because growth is visible far into the future.
claims.quote: So in terms of Visa, I think you can see the company having the most protected for many, many years. It's hard to figure out who could hurt them. And you can see many, many years of growth.
claims.speaker: FRANCOIS ROCHON

claims.claim: The speaker acknowledges Apple is a great business with a solid moat but notes the risk of missing product launches or having a competitor with a better product.
claims.quote: And I think they do have a moat. And probably, five years ago, I wasn't that convinced that the moat was that large. And it turned out that it is a very solid business. And I think-- I don't know exactly the number, but I think, today, 10% of their revenues are service-based and recurring.
claims.speaker: FRANCOIS ROCHON

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Apple's business relies on selling new products every two or three years, creating a risk of missing a launch or failing to satisfy customers.
claims.quote: And when you have to sell something new every two or three years, there's a risk that you'll miss a product launch, or something will not exactly satisfy the customer for whatever reason.
claims.speaker: FRANCOIS ROCHON

claims.claim: The speaker believes Google's business is more stable, entrenched, and recurring than Apple's, and has a larger moat.
claims.quote: So I think, if you compare Apple and Google, I think, Google's business is more stable, and more entrenched, and more recurring. And I think the moat is larger in Google than Apple.
claims.speaker: FRANCOIS ROCHON

claims.claim: The speaker states that Visa trades at a P/E ratio close to 30.
claims.quote: SPEAKER 1: What about Visa? FRANCOIS ROCHON: Visa is close to 30.
claims.speaker: FRANCOIS ROCHON

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Apple trades at a P/E ratio of 15 times.
claims.quote: I think Apple trades at 15 times, and Google is probably 25 times.
claims.speaker: FRANCOIS ROCHON

claims.claim: The speaker estimates that Google trades at a P/E ratio of probably 25 times.
claims.quote: I think Apple trades at 15 times, and Google is probably 25 times.
claims.speaker: FRANCOIS ROCHON

claims.claim: The speaker acknowledges that owning Berkshire Hathaway provides indirect exposure to Apple, but states that this is not a reason not to buy Apple directly if it is a good purchase.
claims.quote: Of course, when we own Berkshire, we own Apple, and we own Coca-Cola, and we own Geico, and some Burlington Northern Santa Fe, and Precision Castparts. And BNSF and Precision Castparts was in the portfolio a few years back.
claims.speaker: FRANCOIS ROCHON
